There is a kind of silence that lives in the space between thoughts, and I have been trying to listen to it all morning. The coffee is cooling in a blue ceramic mug, the one with a chip on the rim that my finger finds without thinking. Outside, the light is the color of unfinished things—pale, tentative, as if the sun hasn't decided whether to commit to the day. I want to write something true, but truth is slippery. It moves like a fish in a shallow stream, visible one moment and gone the next, leaving only the ripple of its passing.

I think about the word *wander*. How it sounds like what it means—a soft, open vowel followed by a stumble, then a return. I wander through sentences the way I wander through rooms, picking up objects, putting them down, forgetting why I came. There is a peculiar freedom in having no destination. The mind, when allowed to drift, finds its own currents. Sometimes those currents carry debris: a scrap of conversation from years ago, the smell of rain on hot pavement, the face of someone I no longer know. Sometimes they carry nothing but the feeling of carrying nothing.

I remember a summer when I was nine. My family rented a cabin by a lake, and every evening I would walk to the end of a wooden dock and lie flat on my back, staring up at the sky. The boards were warm from the day's sun, and the water beneath made a sound like someone breathing slowly. I didn't think about anything. That is a rare thing, to not think about anything. I try to recapture it now, but the adult mind is a crowded room. There are lists to make, worries to fold, plans to revise. The nine-year-old on the dock is a ghost I visit, not a person I can become.

What is it about writing that draws us in? Maybe it is the illusion of control. We cannot shape our lives, but we can shape a paragraph. We can place a comma like a stepping stone, pause at a period, let a sentence run wild until it crashes into a dash—and then stop. Writing is the only place where chaos can be rearranged into meaning, or at least into the appearance of meaning. I think we are all just trying to make sense of the static, the white noise of existence. We take the raw material of days and try to spin it into gold, or at least into something we can hold.

There is a poem I half-remember about how we are all walking each other home. I don't know who wrote it, or if the line is exact. But it feels true. Every conversation is a kind of escort. Every shared silence is a road. We are all carrying small lanterns for one another, even when we don't realize it. The stranger who holds the door, the friend who sends a text at midnight, the barista who writes your name on a cup—they are all guides, leading you a little closer to the place where you feel less alone.

I wonder if anyone is reading this. I wonder if words ever feel like they are meant for a particular pair of eyes, or if they are just thrown into the wind like dandelion seeds. There is an intimacy in writing that is strange and one-sided. You, whoever you are, are inside my head right now. You are hearing the rhythm of my thoughts, the way I pause, the things I choose to share and the things I leave out. That is a kind of trust, even if it is blind. I am trusting you to make something of these words, to find a thread worth following.

The coffee is cold now. I should heat it up, but I don't. There is something honest about cold coffee, a reminder that time has passed, that I have been sitting here for longer than I meant to. The chip on the mug, the pale light outside, the unfinished feeling of the morning—everything is exactly as it should be, which is to say, everything is a little imperfect. Maybe that is the secret. We are always waiting for the perfect moment, the right words, the clear sky. But the perfect moment is a rumor. All we have is this: the half-empty cup, the uncertain light, the page that waits for us to fill it with our stumbling.

I used to think that being a writer meant having something important to say. Now I think it means being willing to say anything, even the unimportant, and to say it with enough attention that it becomes important. A grocery list can be a poem if you read it the right way. A sigh can be a sentence. The word *maybe* can hold an entire world of possibility, if you let it.

There is a bird outside—a small brown one, maybe a sparrow. It is hopping from branch to branch, making a sound that is somewhere between a question and a complaint. I watch it for a while. It doesn't seem to be going anywhere in particular. It is just moving, because moving is what it does. I envy that. To act without the weight of meaning, to simply be a motion in the world, unexamined and free.

But I am human, and humans are meaning-making machines. We cannot help it. We see patterns in stars, faces in clouds, messages in the way a leaf falls. We are always asking *what does it mean?* even when the answer is *nothing, maybe, everything.* And so I keep writing, keep trying to shape the shapeless, keep trying to catch the fish in the stream with my bare hands.

If I reach one thousand words, what will happen? Will the page glow? Will the sky clear? No. I will just stop. I will put down the pen or lift my fingers from the keyboard, and the silence will return. But that is okay. The silence is not empty. It is full of all the words I didn't write, all the thoughts I didn't think, all the mornings when I sat with cold coffee and watched the light change. It is full of you, reader, and the strange, blind trust we share.

I think I am almost there. The word count ticks up like a quiet clock. I could add a story about the time I got lost in a city I didn't know, or a memory about my grandmother's hands, or a joke that only I find funny. But maybe it is better to stop here, in the middle of the thought, the way conversations end when you have to go. There is a beauty in unfinished things. Like the pale morning light, like the bird hopping thoughtlessly, like a sentence that trails off into silence—this is where I leave you. Not with an ending, but with a pause. And in the pause, there is everything.
